title: Modi Slams Climate Blame Game: Developed Nations Emit Six Times More Than India
excerpt: Opening an international environment conference in New Delhi, the prime minister said India is the only G20 nation to have met its Paris climate commitments ahead of schedule.
body:
• Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday inaugurated the two-day international conference “The Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics” in New Delhi, organized by the National Green Tribunal.
  • He said developed nations produce six times more per capita carbon emissions than India, and that blame for climate change is wrongly placed on developing countries.
  • Modi asserted that India is the only G20 nation to have already fulfilled its Paris Agreement commitments ahead of schedule, and said the country is expanding nuclear energy alongside renewables.
  • He criticized environmental activists who, he said, preach about the environment yet move court to block nuclear energy projects.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday accused developed nations of unfairly shifting blame for climate change onto developing countries, telling an international conference in New Delhi that per capita carbon emissions in the developed world remain six times higher than India’s.

Speaking at the inauguration of the two-day international conference, “The Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics,” organized by the National Green Tribunal (NGT), Modi said India’s contribution to per capita carbon emissions is less than half the global average — a fact he said New Delhi presses forcefully on global platforms. He also launched the NGT Mobile App at the event.

“We all know that the responsibility for carbon emissions has often been wrongly placed on developing countries. While the historical truth is that even today, India’s contribution to per capita carbon emissions is less than half of the global average.”

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India

“Six times higher — say it forcefully”

The prime minister returned to the emissions gap several times. “Developed nations have six times more per capita carbon emissions compared to India, and New Delhi strongly presents this fact on global platforms,” he said. “And I would say to every Indian: You too say this forcefully.”

Modi framed the argument as one of historical responsibility: the countries that industrialized first, and emitted the most over the past century, should not shift the burden of climate action onto nations still lifting their populations out of poverty. India, he said, is “working with the rest of the world” while “setting new standards for environmental protection,” and asserted that “our development is both speedy, as well as sustainable.”

India’s climate record

Modi said India is focusing heavily on renewable energy and is the only nation in the G20 that has already fulfilled its Paris (COP21) commitments, well before its timeline. “This is the power of New India. Non-fossil fuels, solar energy capacity, stoppage on carbon emissions... India’s performance on all such metrics is being discussed across the world,” he said.

He also invoked India’s civilizational relationship with nature, saying the country has long drawn on its cultural traditions to promote environmental stewardship and is now combining those values with modern solutions to tackle climate change.

The nuclear jab

The prime minister used the platform to criticize what he described as selective environmental activism at home. India is working at a fast pace on nuclear energy generation, he said — but whenever the government advances nuclear projects, those who preach most loudly about the environment move court to halt them. The remark drew a contrast between opposition to clean nuclear power and the activists’ stated environmental concerns.

Context and background

The NGT conference has brought together judges and judicial representatives from 17 countries, alongside environmental experts, Supreme Court judges, legal experts, and senior government officials, to deliberate on environmental governance, enforcement mechanisms, and institutional cooperation. Discussions are expected to focus on strengthening legal and judicial approaches to climate and environmental challenges.

Modi’s remarks continue a long-running Indian position at climate forums: that per capita and historical emissions, not just current totals, should determine who bears the greatest responsibility for climate action. India has consistently argued that its development needs leave it limited room to cut emissions at the pace demanded by the West — even as it expands solar capacity and non-fossil fuel generation faster than most large economies.

What it means for the diaspora

Modi’s direct appeal — “I would say to every Indian: You too say this forcefully” — was aimed at Indians everywhere, including the diaspora, many of whom take part in climate and policy debates in their adopted countries. For Indian-origin communities in the West, the six-fold emissions gap is a talking point that cuts both ways: it defends India’s development path while pressing wealthy nations to own their outsized historical footprint.

What to watch

The conference continues through Sunday, with deliberations expected to produce recommendations on judicial cooperation in environmental enforcement. Beyond the event, the test of Modi’s argument will come at the next round of international climate negotiations, where India’s demand for differentiated responsibility meets the West’s push for deeper, faster cuts from all major emitters.
